probes.proves: pressing call on a call that is already live changes nothing: same conversation, no teardown, no second bridge answering alongside the first.
hanging up a call that is already down is a no-op, not an error.

turns.prompt: In one sentence: why is the sky blue?
turns.proves: the first answer of a fresh call, asked the instant the bridge says the call is live: a playout that has never opened, a codec that has never been driven, and — from session two on — a mount that was remounted seconds ago. This is where a device that refuses a whole answer as duplicate audio refuses it.
turns.transcript: Rayleigh scattering makes shorter blue wavelengths bend more than longer ones as sunlight passes through the atmosphere. It's the same reason sunsets are red — the scattered blue light is what we see looking up.

turns.prompt: Name one bird that cannot fly. One sentence.
turns.proves: queueing: the next question goes in the moment the previous answer finishes playing, with no settle at all, so a device that needs a breath between turns has nowhere to take it.
turns.transcript: The ostrich is a bird that cannot fly. They have powerful legs for running instead.

turns.transcript: Hello there. How can I help you today?

turns.prompt: In about five sentences, and in your own words, explain how a microphone works.
turns.proves: interrupting an answer that is still playing. The paragraph is cancelled on purpose, so this case is licensed to lose the audio the listener was never going to hear — and the answer that displaces it must still arrive, play, and leave the call healthy.
turns.interruptPrompt: Actually, stop — just tell me one word for the colour of the sea.
turns.transcript: Blue. That's the obvious one, though it can look green or grey too depending on the light and what's in the water.

turns.prompt: In one sentence, what is thunder?
turns.proves: a call that sat saying nothing for half a minute and then had to answer at once. Idle is where a connection quietly dies and where a device parks buffers it will need back.
turns.transcript: Thunder is the sound wave created when lightning superheats the air around it, causing rapid expansion and a shockwave. It's why you hear the boom after seeing the flash.

turns.prompt: Describe a rainy afternoon in a harbour town, in a paragraph of your own.
turns.proves: tearing the call down mid-sentence, which is what a person does when they have heard enough. Licensed to lose the rest of the answer; NOT licensed to leave a stuck call, a wedged playout, or a counter in the never-moves tier moved.
turns.transcript: The rain falls steadily on the harbour, turning the cobblestones slick and darkening the wooden boats tied along the quay. Gulls huddle on the masts while the water laps grey against the stone walls, and a few fishermen in oilskins move quietly between sheds.

counterPolicy.why: the known defect: sustained audio overflows the playout ring and the listener hears a truncated answer. A 90-minute run lost 30% of its audio here. Never allowed, not even inside a cut — raising this is how that run would have 'passed'.
a hole in the frame sequence — audio that never arrived at all.
frames the DAC would not take.
frames the device could not parse.
frames the device could not decode.
microphone frames the device could not send.
transport writes that failed.
transport reads that failed.
a message neither side could make sense of.
inbound work dropped for want of room.
outbound work dropped for want of room.
a liveness probe that went unanswered.
the device restarted its own transport — the session under test was replaced underneath it.
the device lost the bridge holding its call.
captured speech the device threw away.
button reads the device could not complete (older firmware calls it talkReadFailures).
the pre-rename name of lowerReadFailures.
an audible gap: the ring ran dry while the DAC was open. Cancelling an answer empties that ring by design, so the two cut cases may move it; a clean turn may not.
concealment papering over a missing frame — audible. Same licence as underruns, for the same reason.

the DAC was handed a cleared buffer MID-ANSWER — audible starvation, and now that the answer-end drain is counted separately (dmaDraining) there is no innocent explanation left for it. Fatal on any turn, cut or not.

cleared descriptors the hardware sent after the source went dry — the normal end of every answer. The ring is 90ms deep and the speaker task waits 60ms for a frame that is not coming, so this moves 5-12 times per short turn on a turn where every frame sent was played. It used to land in dmaUnderruns, which is what disqualified session 1.
frames the playout threw away. On a cut that is the answer being abandoned; on a clean turn it is a truncated answer.

one per answer, always: every answer begins by displacing the last, so the device's own REPLACE path fires on a perfect turn. This was published as spkReplaced and tiered as a fault, which made every clean turn look damaged. The subset that actually costs audio is spkSupersededMidplay.
an answer displaced while it was STILL PLAYING — queued audio thrown away. This is what a barge-in does deliberately and what nothing else may do.
frames refused for belonging to an answer that has been superseded.
frames refused for belonging to a call that has ended — the hang-up case in one number.

frames refused as duplicates. Measured once eating a WHOLE first answer of a call started right after a previous one, which is precisely the boundary this command crosses ten times — so on a clean turn it fails the run.
the playout skipped ahead to pay off lag: heard as a stutter, so never acceptable on a clean turn.
the other half of catch-up accounting; same reasoning.

one per answer, always: the source going dry IS how an answer ends. Published as spkWaitDry and tiered as a fault on the belief it measured zero across a 26-minute call; it measured 62 across 62 turns, which is once each.
the device counting its own interruptions. Expected on the barge-in case and nowhere else.
the DAC opens once per answer; it moves on every healthy turn.
ticks while the playout waits to prime; already in the hundreds of thousands on an idle device.
work deferred to the next tick rather than dropped — back-pressure working as designed.
make-before-break replacement of the downlink connection. It loses nothing, and if it ever did, the sent-equals-played gate would say so.
